entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titus Genucius Augurinus, a Roman patrician of the Gens Genucia, rose to prominence in the mid-5th century BC, serving as consul in 451 BC and subsequently as a key member of the first decemvirate. His career unfolded during a pivotal era for the nascent Roman Republic, marked by intense socio-political struggles between the entrenched patrician aristocracy and the burgeoning plebeian class, particularly concerning the transparency and application of law. His involvement in the codification of the Twelve Tables, Rome's foundational legal document, cemented his place in Roman legal and political history.

Elected consul alongside Appius Claudius Crassus in 451 BC, Titus Genucius Augurinus then played an instrumental role in the extraordinary governmental body known as the Decemviri Legibus Scribundis, or "Ten Men for Writing Laws." This commission, granted supreme authority and superseding ordinary magistracies, was tasked with drafting a written legal code to address the plebeians' demands for legal certainty and protection against arbitrary patrician judgments. The first decemvirate, under Augurinus's participation, successfully produced the initial ten tables of what would become the Twelve Tables, which were publicly displayed in the Roman Forum for all citizens to consult.
